qt: to the Commission Mathilde Androuët (ID) Subject:

A recent study by the French health authorities suggests that the risk of having menstrual disorders increases in the three months following the administration of an mRNA COVID vaccine1. It reveals that there is ‘a 20 % increase in the risk of heavy menstrual bleeding requiring hospitalisation within 1 to 3 months’ after receiving the Pfizer or Moderna vaccine for the first time. After having put huge efforts into promoting COVID-19 vaccination campaigns, it is time for the Commission to help further the scientific research on the potential harm of these vaccines to women. 1.
What action will the Commission take to further monitor and assess these potential effects on women’s health?

With this in mind, how will it strengthen cooperation with national health authorities and regulatory bodies to collect reliable and independent data on possible side effects, in particular on women’s health?
How will it communicate transparently about these issues to ensure that the public is clearly informed and any concerns are addressed?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (18.6.2024) 1. The safety and the efficacy of COVID-19 vaccines authorised in the EU, including their potential effects on women’s health, has always been a priority of the Commission. The European Medicines Agency (EMA) assessed in 2022 a safety signal on heavy menstrual bleedings1 and recommended to update the product information of the Spikevax and Comirnaty to include heavy menstrual bleeding as a side effect. 2. A strong pharmacovigilance system with cooperation between the Member States, the EMA and the Commission is in place for COVID-19 vaccines2 to continuously monitor their safety and to ensure any possible risks are detected and managed as early as possible. 3. All reports of suspected side effects are promptly assessed by regulatory authorities and, if appropriate, the Commission takes regulatory action based on EMA’s recommendation, including, if necessary, risk-minimisation measures based on gender. Side effects are included in the publicly available vaccine product information3, the European Public Assessment Report4 and periodic safety update reports (PSURs)5,6, to ensure that healthcare professionals and patients have up-to-date information.
1 Meeting highlights from the Pharmacovigilance Risk Assessment Committee (PRAC) 24 - 27 October 2022:
